archetype.name: Retooling (run-first, pass-broken)
archetype.definition: A team a year removed from a top-10 offense whose passing game and turnover margin have fallen apart, leaving a sound run game and a stingy third-down defense with nothing to hold onto.

report.headline: A good run game buried under a broken passing attack and turnovers.
report.take:
The Colts are 2-6, but the record and the profile point the same way: this is a below-average team, not an unlucky one. The point differential sits at -61 and implies only 3.2 wins, so the bounces have cost them about a game (winsOverExpected -1.24). The bigger story is how lopsided the roster is playing. The run game is one of the league's best by efficiency (run EPA 4th, rushing EPA per play 5th), Jonathan Taylor carries a heavy load with 148 carries, and the offense owns the ball (time of possession 5th). The passing game, with Daniel Jones starting every week, ranks 31st in EPA per dropback. That is the season.

The turnover margin turns a bad passing offense into a losing team. Indianapolis has given the ball away 15 times and taken it away 4 times, a -11 margin that ranks last in the league per game. The defense is not the problem it looks like on the scoreboard. It ranks 4th at getting off the field on third down (30% allowed) and 10th in success rate allowed. But it barely touches the quarterback (pressure rate 29th), rarely takes the ball away (31st), and gets leaned on by the run (rush EPA allowed 28th). It is a bend-but-stop-on-third unit that keeps getting handed short fields and extra possessions.

History says the passing collapse is new, not a trend. Last year's Colts went 8-9 with the 7th-best offensive EPA and an even turnover margin. This year's team still does the small things well: the fewest penalties per game in the league and a top-10 special teams unit. The decline has also gotten worse as the schedule toughened. Since a 2-2 start they haven't won, and the 7-42 loss at Jacksonville produced a -21.3 passing EPA, the worst passing game of the season.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the passing game can just reach mediocre. The remaining slate is soft in places, with Miami, Philadelphia and Tennessee all near the bottom. A team that runs this well and wins on third down should steal games if it stops giving the ball away. Jacksonville sits at 5-2, so the division is gone in all but math, and the realistic goal is respectability and an answer at quarterback.

strengths.title: An efficient, physical run game
strengths.body: The ground game is a real top-five unit by efficiency, not a product of game script, because they have been trailing most of the year and still run it well. The line creates room at a league-average rate and Taylor turns it into positive plays. It carried the Week 4 win at Washington with a 7.9 rushing EPA while the passing game sank. The line's quality makes it repeatable.

strengths.title: Third-down defense gets off the field
strengths.body: Holding opponents to 30% on third down, 4th best, is why the defense grades mid-pack despite little pass rush and few takeaways. The tight coverage on outside receivers helps here: WR1s and WR2s have struggled against them. Third-down rates swing year to year, so some regression is likely, especially with two corners out.

strengths.title: Clean, ball-control football
strengths.body: The fewest penalties per game in the league, a 5th-ranked time of possession and an 8th-ranked special teams unit give them a floor in close games. This is coaching and discipline, which tends to hold up all season.

concerns.title: Passing game near the league floor
concerns.body: At -0.187 EPA per dropback, 31st, the passing game wipes out what the run game builds. Jones is also absorbing hits: 23 sacks and the 30th-ranked hit rate allowed, while the line is middle of the pack on pressure rate. That suggests holding the ball and poor decisions, not only blocking. Last year's offense ranked 7th, so the talent around him isn't the obvious cause, and without a quarterback change this looks structural.

concerns.title: A turnover margin sinking the season
concerns.body: Fifteen giveaways against four takeaways is a last-place margin, and it explains why points allowed outrun a defense that is only mildly below average by EPA. Part of this is noise: takeaways that rare usually bounce back somewhat. The giveaways are tied to the passing game, though, so they are less likely to fix themselves.

concerns.title: No pass rush, soft against the run
concerns.body: A 29th-ranked pressure rate means quarterbacks get time, and a 28th-ranked rush EPA allowed means teams can run on them too. Slot receivers, tight ends and backs have been the soft spots in coverage. With Justin Walley out and Cam Taylor-Britt on IR, the depth in the back end gets tested.

trend.note: A 2-2 start built on a gritty Houston win and a run-driven rout of Washington has given way to a winless stretch. It bottomed out with a 7-42 loss at Jacksonville, the worst passing performance of the year.

nextGame.headline: Colts' run game meets the league's leakiest defense
nextGame.body:
Dallas is the mirror image of Indianapolis: a 4th-ranked offense with the league's lowest sack rate allowed, paired with a defense ranked last by play-by-play EPA and 30th against both pass and run. The Book has Dallas -6 with a 51.5 total and the Colts at +220, which prices this as a Dallas shootout. The Colts' best counter is the opposite script: run at a defense that has been gashed, win time of possession (they rank 5th, Dallas 30th), and keep Dak Prescott on the sideline. Dallas's defense is the one unit on the schedule that might let Jones look competent, since it ranks last in third-down defense and allows big days to opposing WR1s.

Availability tilts slightly toward the Colts on defense' opposite side. Dallas has both safeties in the concussion protocol, including Caleb Downs at 93% of snaps. Linebacker Dee Winters is out, Malachi Lawrence is questionable and Marist Liufau is on IR, so the second level of a weak run defense is thin. Tight end Jake Ferguson is questionable with an ankle sprain. The Colts, though, play without corner Justin Walley and linebacker Bryce Boettcher, with Cam Taylor-Britt on IR. That weakens a secondary that already struggles against slot receivers, tight ends and backs.

waysToWin.title: Feed Taylor, own the clock
waysToWin.body: The Colts' 4th-ranked run EPA against Dallas's 30th-ranked rush defense, missing linebackers, is the clearest edge on the board. Long drives shorten the game and limit Dallas's possessions, which is how a 6-point underdog with a weak pass rush keeps a top-four offense under 30.

waysToWin.title: Josh Downs against a soft WR1 defense
waysToWin.body: Dallas has allowed WR1s 6.9 PPR points over their average, 31st, and ranks last on third down. If Jones can keep it simple and target Downs on manageable downs, the drives the run game starts can finish with touchdowns, not field goals. Dallas's red-zone defense ranks 26th.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover coin flip
waysToWin.body: Dallas has forced only 4 takeaways, 30th, so the giveaway problem may ease this week. If the Colts play clean and their third-down defense steals a couple of stops, the game stays within reach.

waysToLose.title: Prescott throws from a clean pocket
waysToLose.body: Dallas allows the lowest sack rate in the league, and the Colts rank 29th in pressure rate. With two corners out, Prescott can work the middle of the field, where slot receivers and backs have hurt Indianapolis.

waysToLose.title: Falling behind, forced to throw
waysToLose.body: If Dallas's 4th-ranked offense scores early, the Colts lose the run-heavy script and have to lean on a 31st-ranked passing game. That is how the Jacksonville game turned into a rout.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways hand over short fields
waysToLose.body: Even against a defense that rarely forces turnovers, the Colts have had multiple giveaways in most games. Against an offense this efficient, each one is close to points.

nextGame.watch: How many carries Taylor gets in the first half: if the Colts are still running on early downs at halftime, they are playing the game they can win.

restOfSeason.body:
Two things should get better. The takeaway count is extremely low for a defense that wins on third down and ranks 10th in success rate allowed, and a schedule with Miami, Philadelphia and Tennessee left offers real chances to win. The run game and the discipline are built to last.

The passing game is the ceiling. Nothing in the dossier suggests a fix short of a quarterback change: a 31st-ranked dropback EPA and a high hit rate point to the passer as much as the protection. Expect a team that wins some of the soft games on the ground, loses to Cincinnati and Jacksonville, and finishes with a losing record well behind Jacksonville in the division.
swingFactors: Whether Daniel Jones keeps the job or the passing game stabilizes
Turnover luck turning on the takeaway side
Health of a secondary already missing two corners

confidence.note: Eight games with a consistent profile and the same quarterback; turnover swings add noise.
